'''David Hudson Staelin''' (1938 – 2011) was an American astronomer, engineer, and entrepreneur. He co-discovered the [[Crab Pulsar|Crab nebula pulsar]] in 1968, and was [[Principal Investigator]] for earth-[[remote-sensing]] satellite instruments. He was a co-founder of Environmental Research and Technology, Inc. and the founding chairman of [[PictureTel Corp.]], one of the first [[Videotelephony|videoconferencing]] firms.

== Early life and education ==
Staelin grew up in [[Ottawa Hills, Ohio]], a suburb of [[Toledo, Ohio|Toledo]].<ref name="blade">Zaborney, M., [https://www.toledoblade.com/news/deaths/2011/12/02/David-H-Staelin-1938-2011-Researcher-at-MIT-was-an-Ottawa-Hills-native/stories/201112020077 "David H. Staelin, 1938-2011: Researcher at MIT was an Ottawa Hills native"], Toledo Blade, Dec. 2, 2011.</ref>
He was the oldest of four children in his family.<ref name="globe">Lawrence, J. M., [https://www.bostonglobe.com/metro/obituaries/2011/12/12/david-staelin-scientist-discoverer-entrepreneur/c0IYlvz6nIp3NgQlsaESTK/story.html "David Staelin, 73, scientist, discoverer, entrepreneur"], Boston Globe, December 12, 2011.</ref>
After graduating from [[Ottawa Hills High School (Ohio)|Ottawa Hills High School]], he enrolled at the [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]] (MIT) and received a Bachelor of Science degree in electrical engineering in 1960, then a Master of Science degree in 1961 and Doctor of Science degree in electrical engineering in 1965, all from MIT.<ref name="mit">[http://news.mit.edu/2011/obit-staelin-1115 "David Staelin, longtime professor in EECS and RLE, dies at 73"], MIT News Office, Nov. 15, 2011.</ref>

== Career ==
That same year (1965) he joined the faculty of the Electrical Engineering and Computer Science department and the [[radio astronomy]] group of the Research Laboratory of Electronics at MIT. He remained on the faculty at MIT for the rest of his life. He also served as an assistant director of  [[MIT Lincoln Laboratory]] from 1990 to 2001. From 2003 to 2005, he was a member of the U.S. President's Information Technology Advisory Committee.<ref name="mit" />

While on leave at the [[National Radio Astronomy Observatory]] in 1968, Staelin developed the computationally efficient [[fast folding algorithm]]<ref>{{Citation | last=Staelin | first=David H. | title=Fast Folding Algorithm for Detection of Periodic Pulse Trains | journal=Proceedings of the IEEE | volume=57 | issue=4 | pages=724–5 | date=1969 |doi=10.1109/PROC.1969.7051| bibcode=1969IEEEP..57..724S }}</ref>
for detection of periodic signals, which enabled him and Edward C. Reifenstein III to find two [[pulsar]]s in the vicinity of the [[Crab Nebula]], which were close enough to it (given the [[angular resolution]] of the antenna) to potentially be associated with it.<ref>{{Citation | last1=Staelin | first1=David H. | last2=Reifenstein, III | first2=Edward C. | title=Pulsating radio sources near the Crab Nebula | journal=Science | volume=162 | pages=1481–3 | date=1968 |doi=10.1126/science.162.3861.1481 | pmid=17739779 | issue=3861 | jstor=1725616 |bibcode = 1968Sci...162.1481S| s2cid=38023534 }}</ref>
One of these, NP 0532, was subsequently determined to be at the center of the nebula.<ref>{{Citation |last1=Reifenstein, III |first1=Edward C. | last3=Staelin | first3=David H. | last2=Brundage | first2=William D. | title=Crab Nebula Pulsar NPO527 | date=1969 | journal=[[Physical Review Letters]] | volume=22 | issue=7 | pages=311 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.22.311 | bibcode=1969PhRvL..22..311R}}</ref>
The first astronomical pulsar had been discovered by [[Jocelyn Bell Burnell]] and [[Antony Hewish]] in 1967,<ref>{{Citation | last1=Hewish | first1=Antony | last2=Bell | first2=S. J.| last3=Pilkington | first3=J. D. H.|last4=Scott | first4=P. F.| last5=Collins|first5=R. A.| title=Observation of a Rapidly Pulsating Radio Source| journal=Nature| volume=217| issue=5130 | pages=709–13 | date=1968 |doi=10.1038/217709a0| bibcode=1968Natur.217..709H| s2cid=4277613 }}</ref>
but the origin of such pulsating radio signals had not yet been established. The association of a pulsar with the Crab Nebula, which was known to be the remnant of a [[supernova]],<ref>{{cite book |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=r47qBwAAQBAJ&pg=PA196 |pages=196–200 |title=A History of Astronomy: from 1890 to the Present |first=David|last= Leverington |publisher=Springer Science and Business Media |year=2012|isbn=9781447121244}}</ref>
supported the hypothesis<ref>{{Citation | last = Gold | first = T. | title = Rotating Neutron Stars as the Origin of the Pulsating Radio Sources| journal = Nature| volume = 218| pages = 731–732| year = 1968| doi = 10.1038/218731a0| bibcode=1968Natur.218..731G | issue=5143| s2cid = 4217682 }}</ref>
that pulsars are rotating [[neutron star]]s, and provided observational evidence that a neutron star could result from a supernova explosion.<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.cv.nrao.edu/~sransom/web/Ch6.html |title=Essential Radio Astronomy (Sec.6.2) |publisher=National Radio Astronomy Observatory |accessdate=September 2, 2020 |first1=J. J. |last1=Condon |first2=S. M. |last2=Ransom}}</ref>

He proposed two [[microwave]] spectrometers for [[remote-sensing]] of the Earth, which were flown on the [[Nimbus 5]] and [[Nimbus 6]] satellites, respectively.<ref>{{Citation | last=Staelin | first=D. H.|display-authors=etal| title=Microwave Spectrometer on the Nimbus 5 Satellite: Meteorological and Geophysical Data | journal=Science| volume=182 | pages=1339–41 | date=1973 | issue=4119|doi=10.1126/science.182.4119.1339| pmid=17733112| bibcode=1973Sci...182.1339S| s2cid=32789771}}</ref><ref>{{Citation | last1=Staelin | first1=D. H. | last2=Rosenkranz | first2=P. W. | last3=Barath | first3=F. T.|last4=Johnston | first4=E. J.| last5=Waters|first5=J. W.| title=Microwave Spectroscopic Imagery of the Earth | journal=Science| volume=197 | pages=991–3 | date=1977 | issue=4307 |doi=10.1126/science.197.4307.991| pmid=17784136 | bibcode=1977Sci...197..991S | s2cid=37769601 }}</ref>
These experimental instruments could measure [[atmospheric temperature]] profiles even in the presence of clouds that blocked the view of [[infrared]] instruments,<ref>{{Citation | last=Staelin | first=D. H. |display-authors=etal | title=Microwave Atmospheric Temperature Sounding: Effects of Clouds on the Nimbus 5 Satellite Data | journal=Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences| volume=32 |issue=10 | pages=1970–6 | date=1975 |doi=10.1175/1520-0469(1975)032<1970:MATSEO>2.0.CO;2| bibcode=1975JAtS...32.1970S | doi-access=free }}</ref>
and they were forerunners of subsequent microwave [[atmospheric sounding]] instruments ([[Microwave sounding unit|MSU]], [[Advanced microwave sounding unit|AMSU]], [[Advanced Technology Microwave Sounder|ATMS]]) on [[NOAA]] and [[EUMETSAT]] [[weather satellite]]s.<ref>{{cite conference | last= Blackwell| first=W. J. | title=Approaching 50 Years of Earth Atmospheric Sensing from Space Using Passive Microwave Observations: A Retrospective |conference=American Meteorological Society 96th Annual Meeting|location=New Orleans, LA, 10–14 January 2016 |url=https://ams.confex.com/ams/96Annual/webprogram/Paper291095.html}}</ref>

In 1968 Staelin and Norman E. Gaut founded Environmental Research and Technology, Inc. (acquired by [[AECOM]] in 1979), a company which specialized in air-quality measurements and became "one of the largest air quality monitoring sources in the world".<ref name="globe"/> 
In the 1980s Staelin began to investigate [[videoconferencing]] as an alternative to travel. An outgrowth of his research in this area was the founding in 1984 of PicTel Corporation (renamed [[PictureTel Corp.]] in 1987; acquired by [[Polycom]] in 2001), by Staelin and his former students [[Brian Hinman]] and Jeffrey G. Bernstein.<ref>Gilpin, K. N. and Schmitt, E.,[https://www.nytimes.com/1986/01/16/business/business-people-13-engineers-at-pictel-meet-phone-deadline.html "BUSINESS PEOPLE; 13 Engineers at Pictel Meet Phone Deadline"], New York Times, Jan. 16, 1986, Section D, Page 2.</ref> <!--Note: Jeffrey is the correct spelling; the name is misspelled in the Times article.-->

He was a co-investigator for the Planetary Radio Astronomy instrument on the [[Voyager 1]] and [[Voyager 2]] missions to [[Jupiter]], [[Saturn]], [[Uranus]] and [[Neptune]],<ref>{{Citation | last1=Warwick | first1=J.W. |last2=Pearce|first2=J.B.|last3=Peltzer|first3=R.G.|last4=Riddle|first4=A.C.| title=Planetary radio astronomy experiment for Voyager missions | journal=Space Science Reviews| volume=21 | pages=309–327 | date=1977 | issue=3 |doi=10.1007/BF00211544| bibcode=1977SSRv...21..309W | s2cid=120778786 }}</ref> and a member of the science team for the [[Atmospheric Infrared Sounder]] on NASA's [[Aqua satellite]].<ref>[https://airs.jpl.nasa.gov/ AIRS]</ref>

== Personal life ==
He had two brothers, Earl and Stephen Staelin and a sister, Mimi Ferrell. He married Ellen Mahoney, and they had three children, Carl, Katharine and Paul.<ref name="globe"/>

== Honors and awards ==
* Fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]
* Fellow of the [[Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers]] (IEEE)
* 1996 Distinguished Achievement Award of the [[IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Society]]
* 2011 John Howard Dellinger Medal of the [[International Union of Radio Science]]

== Books ==
* Staelin, D. H.; Morgenthaler, A. W.; and Kong, J. A. (1993), ''Electromagnetic Waves'' (Prentice-Hall) {{ISBN|0-13-225871-4}}
* Staelin, D. H. and Staelin, C. H. (2011), ''Models for Neural Spike Computation and Cognition'', (www.cognon.net) {{ISBN|9781466472228}}
